Well that's not good. The problem is on the main board then. If the main board can be removed without too much trouble, I would look at the solder connections for the z-axis connector to make sure they are still good. If you have a soldering iron and solder, maybe flow some new solder onto the connector pins to ensure they are solid. A hairline solder break could look like a good connection but be electrically broken causing one coil to not fire. If this does not fix it, trace the lines back to their source and if you have a multimeter with a continuity check, test it by putting a probe at both ends to see if you get a tone from one end to the other. If it's got continuity then something is dead unfortunately. If no continuity, well look for breaks in the trace or solder a new wire from one end to the other to see if it fixes the problem. My hope is that it's just a cold solder joint at the connector but you'll only know for sure if you can reflow the joints to make them solid or get a continuity test done.

Depending on how your controller and drivers are setup the motor could be driven in a microstepping mode which would use multiple coils to drive the motor on each step. This would mean losing a whole coil/phase would not be completely detrimental to its movement but would certainly affect its accuracy, speed, torque and overall smoothness of motion. You could probably get a feel for it if you hold the belt/pulley to see if putting some resistance on it causes noticeable step loss. If you try this, do it on multiple axes to know what a good axis feels like versus the bad axis. If you have an oscilloscope you could also test each motor coil to see if it is getting pulses which would nail down a bad trace/output. An LED and a series resistor could also suffice is you don't have a scope but it may be difficult to see since the pulses will be short. A multimeter might catch it too if it has a high enough sampling rate. Ultimately it does seem that the coil outputs must be tested in order to move on to the next step in troubleshooting. Until it is known whether or not you have a bad output it's difficult to know where to move next. Hopefully one of these methods will help discover what went wrong.
